props.title: Monkey Business

sections.content: Howard Hawks' screwball comedy Monkey Business brilliantly pairs Cary Grant and Ginger Rogers in a madcap exploration of aging, youth, and scientific mishaps. Grant plays Dr. Barnaby Fulton, a chemist who accidentally discovers a youth serum that sends both him and his wife through increasingly chaotic personality regressions. The film builds on Hawks' earlier screwball masterpieces like Bringing Up Baby (1938) and His Girl Friday (1940), maintaining that rapid-fire dialogue and physical comedy while adding a clever scientific twist that speaks to 1950s anxieties about modern chemistry and aging.

sections.content: The film's exploration of chemical transformation connects it to a rich tradition of Hollywood scientists-gone-wild narratives. While Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde (1941) took a darker approach, Monkey Business plays its scientific mishaps for laughs while still maintaining subtle commentary on marriage, aging, and professional ambition. Marilyn Monroe's supporting role as a ditzy secretary adds another layer of youth/age contrast, coming just before her breakout roles in Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953) and The Seven Year Itch (1955). SUBHEAD: The Science Comedy Evolution

Monkey Business helped establish a specific comedy subgenre about scientific experiments gone wrong that would influence films for decades. Its DNA can be seen in everything from The Nutty Professor (1963) to Weird Science (1985) and even modern variations like Flubber (1997). The film's particular genius lies in how it uses its premise to explore relationship dynamics - as Grant and Rogers regress to younger versions of themselves, their marriage faces both hilarious and genuinely insightful challenges.
